lessons.title: From the g tensor to direction-dependent resonance
lessons.summary: Rotating the magnetic field around the same spin center changes both resonance positions and microwave matrix elements.

sections.title: Distinguish energy, frequency and magnetic field first
sections.text: Here the Hamiltonian is written as H/h in GHz; magnetic fields are entered in T. μB/h is approximately 13.996245 GHz/T and g is a dimensionless effective tensor. Resonance frequency is the level difference divided by h; do not multiply by another 2π.

sections.title: Read anisotropy together with its orientation
sections.text: gX, gY and gZ are three parameters along common crystal principal axes. theta is measured from z, and phi is the azimuth in the xy plane. For S=½ with no nuclear spin or other interactions, the energy gap depends only on |g n|; at a given B, the z and x directions give different resonances. In more general models, the displayed geometric g_eff cannot replace full diagonalization.
sections.formula: ν=(μB/h) B g_eff；g_eff²=gX² nx²+gY² ny²+gZ² nz²

sections.title: Transition intensity must also be calculated
sections.text: The microwave-field polarizations theta and phi are perpendicular to the static field; parallel is aligned with it. The transition matrix elements include g and the microwave-field direction. In a purely isotropic Zeeman model, longitudinal driving commutes with H, so there is no finite-frequency absorption. This conclusion cannot be carried over directly when anisotropy or state mixing is present.

lessons.title: How zero-field and hyperfine interactions alter spin spectra
lessons.summary: Check energy levels against hand-solvable limits, then observe mixing and splitting under an external field.

sections.title: Which spins admit second-order zero-field splitting?
sections.text: The D term distinguishes mS=0 from mS=±1; the E term mixes states whose spin projections differ by two. For S=1/2, both second-order operators vanish identically, so changing D/E cannot split an isolated Kramers doublet. This page retains only these two second-order parameters and does not include arbitrary higher-order crystal-field operators.

sections.title: An electron and one nuclear spin
sections.text: One nuclear spin I can be included. A⊥ controls transverse spin flips and A∥ longitudinal coupling. Nuclear Zeeman coupling uses −γN B·I, with signed γN in GHz/T. For S=I=½, B=0, and isotropic A, the analytic levels are F=0 and F=1; finite fields mix different total spins.

sections.title: Do not treat effective parameters as automatic outputs
sections.text: The many-electron tool can give a ground-state S within specified approximations, but S alone does not determine g, D, E, or A. Downfolding these parameters also needs SOC, orbital states, a low-energy subspace, and a projection convention. The cross-module assignment first confirms S=1 in the d⁸ model, then studies an effective-spin spectrum using explicitly given parameters; this is not a fitted NiO spectrum.
sections.formula: Many-electron low-energy subspace → explicit projection and SOC → effective-spin parameters

lessons.title: From energy levels to observable absorption: occupation, polarization, and sampling
lessons.summary: Energy differences give candidate frequencies; actual spectral lines also require matrix elements, thermal populations and adequate sampling.

sections.title: Keep thermal populations in the spectral weights
sections.text: Thermal equilibrium occupations use Boltzmann weights. Subtracting stimulated emission from absorption gives a net pi−pf factor for every positive-frequency transition; heating reduces the occupation difference of a pure Zeeman doublet. Spectra are not normalized to equal peak heights, allowing temperature effects to be compared at otherwise fixed parameters.

sections.title: Do not select an arbitrary individual eigenvector from a degenerate level
sections.text: Numerical eigenvectors may rotate arbitrarily within a degenerate subspace. This page sums squared matrix elements between two energy groups and assigns equal populations to degenerate states; at T=0, the weight is distributed uniformly over the entire ground-state subspace. Spectral lines therefore do not depend on the solver’s choice of basis.
sections.formula: WAB=(pA−pB) Tr(PA M† PB M PA)

sections.title: Linewidth and mesh have different roles
sections.text: lineWidth is the Lorentzian half-width at half-maximum in GHz; each line is normalized to unit area on the positive-frequency axis. Coarser grids are more likely to miss narrow peaks. The program compares numerical integration with the analytic area over the same window. This is weak-excitation single-crystal frequency absorption, not the usual field-modulated first-derivative spectrum, and excludes saturation and relaxation.

lessons.title: How hole reflection sends charges into superconductors
lessons.summary: Distinguishes electron/hole probabilities, quasiparticle fluxes, and charge conductance, and fixes counting of physical spins.

sections.title: First identify the two degrees of freedom of the same model
sections.text: uses the (e↑, h↓) Nambu block, and the normal region does not mix electrons and holes; the real s-wave pairing of the right electrode couples the two. Another spin block gives the same probability, so the final conductance is multiplied by 2. Nambu's electron/hole redundancy is not extra physical spin per se.

sections.title: There is no quasiparticle propagating to the right in the subgap
sections.text: When the energy is less than the superconducting energy gap, the ideal electrode has no propagable bulk quasiparticles, but the electron from the left can be reflected as a hole. The condensate undertakes the corresponding charge transfer. Limited bandwidth, potential barriers, and contact mismatches simultaneously produce normal reflections.

sections.title: Hole reflection takes the plus sign in conductance
sections.text: The holes returning to the left and the electrons entering to the right contribute the same sign to the charge current. Therefore, the right electrode quasiparticle transmission T_{qp} cannot be directly regarded as the charge conductance. The response of each incident spin channel is 1−R_{ee}+R_{he}, and two spins have been counted on this page.

sections.title: Conditions required for ideal doubling
sections.text: is in transparent contact, the Fermi energy is far away from the band edge and the Δ relative bandwidth is small, the subgap Andreev reflection is close to 1, and G is close to 4e²/h; the same normal line is 2e²/h. The lattice model has limited bandwidth, and even a contact match does not have to be exactly 4.
sections.formula: Matched lattice interface at μ=E=0: R_{he}=4t²/(4t²+Δ²)

lessons.title: Spectral conductance from normal state scattering to superconducting junctions
lessons.summary: compares normal limits, pairings and barriers for the same device by changing only one physical condition.

sections.title: Δ=0 should return to the existing normal device
sections.text: The normal region is a uniform chain, and both leads have hopping t. μ enters electron and hole onsite energies with opposite signs. Set μ=0 and Δ=0 to compare with the existing device tool. The device-perfect preset counts one spin only, so divide this page’s conductance by 2 before comparing.

sections.title: Potential barrier changes two reflections at the same time
sections.text: When V is increased at a normal site, electrons feel +V and holes feel −V. After the normal state transmission is reduced, the zero-energy Andreev reflection usually decreases faster under the short junction and small energy gap approximation; the specific curve is still calculated by the complete model.
sections.formula: R_{he}(0)≈T_N²/(2−T_N)², suitable for normal scattering that is approximately constant within the Δ window

sections.title: The same reference line retains all normal parameters
sections.text: diagram only sets Δ to 0; the number of sites, μ, potential barriers, contacts, and eta are all unchanged. If both the barrier and the energy gap are changed, the difference cannot be attributed to the pairing alone. The energy is relative to the chemical potential of the superconducting condensate, rather than refilling the entire device with each energy.

sections.title: Spectral conductance and finite bias calculation are separated
sections.text: This page displays the spectral differential conductance corresponding to E under zero temperature, fixed potential and fixed pairing approximation. E=0 is a strictly zero-bias linear conductance; non-zero E can be related to eV under the freezing potential approximation, but the potential, occupation or pairing self-consistency under real bias is not sought.
sections.formula: E=0: linear G; E≠0: fixed potential spectrum dI/dV

lessons.title: Verification of NS results using particle-hole symmetry and flux
lessons.summary: retains threshold empty points and tests surface Green function, artificial absorption and particle-hole relationship.

sections.title: Choose the correct root for retarded boundaries
sections.text: Two semi-infinite leads enter the contact self-energies through surface Green functions. The normal chain uses the exact square-root branch; the superconducting chain uses an analytical rational expression from the same spectral measure. Inside the gap, the right-lead Γ is zero; artificial lead broadening is not used to create propagating channels.

sections.title: Numerical η must be included in the conservation balance
sections.text: Positive eta in the finite normal zone gives artificial absorption A_η. Only by adding it together with the two reflections and the right-hand quasi-particle transmission can the numerical conservation be checked. The stability of reducing eta and the energy scan resolution are two different checks.

sections.title: Electrons and holes of different energies correspond to each other
sections.text: In this block convention, the τy complex conjugation transformation relates E to −E. The normal/Andreev reflection for an electron incident at E should be equal to the corresponding result for a hole incident at −E; you should not just check whether a curve looks symmetrical.

sections.title: Threshold null value is not zero conductance
sections.text: The ideal right electrode needs to carefully take the threshold limit at precise E=±Δ. This version of the analytical formula leaves these points blank, and the sweep curve retains breakpoints. One can approach and check eta from both sides without filling in the nulls with zeros or claiming to have real missing spectra.

lessons.title: From unified J to complete Slater with core hole
lessons.summary: Clarify the difference between the two interactions, and then establish the complete multi-electron space before and after absorption.

sections.title: is also a d shell, and the information retained can be different.
sections.text: The Kanamori lessons use a common J for interorbital exchange. This module constructs the full rotationally invariant d–d Coulomb interaction from spherical-harmonic angular matrices and F⁰, F² and F⁴. F² and F⁴ control different angular channels and are not each equal to a single Hund parameter. Fully antisymmetric fermionic determinants are used.
sections.formula: H_dd=½Σ_abcd U_abcd c†_a c†_b c_d c_c；k=0,2,4

sections.title: The before and after absorption are not in the same configuration space.
sections.text: A 2p core electron is excited into 3d: a d⁸ ion starts in p⁶d⁸, of dimension 45, and ends in p⁵d⁹, of dimension 60. Final states include 2p SOC, direct p–d F⁰/F² and exchange G¹/G³. The d⁹ initial space has dimension 10 and the p⁵d¹⁰ final space dimension 6. In these closed-shell or single-hole configurations, p–p interactions contribute only a common constant, absorbed into the uncalibrated absorption-edge zero.

sections.title: How to read spin and orbital quantities with SOC
sections.text: Valence-shell SOC is the sum of individual-electron l·s operators and cannot be replaced arbitrarily by total L·S without projection. General crystal fields and SOC mix different L and S, so the level table reports ⟨S²⟩, ⟨L²⟩ and degeneracy-averaged occupancies without imposing LS-term labels. Cubic and axial crystal fields are defined in real orbitals related exactly to the spherical-harmonic basis by a change of basis.

lessons.title: Derive polarization selection rules from dipole matrix elements
lessons.summary: The energy difference determines the position of the spectral line, and the wave function and light polarization jointly determine the intensity of the spectral line.

sections.title: Calculate the amplitude first, then square it
sections.text: The electric dipole transition is described by ε·r, 2p→3d changes orbital parity and the dipole operator itself does not flip the spin; SOC mixes the spin components in the ground and final states. The existence of an energy difference does not guarantee the existence of non-zero transition strengths. The radial dipole integral on this page is fixed to 1, and the angular matrix elements and multi-electron antisymmetry are retained.

sections.title: Compare linear polarization and circular polarization
sections.text: x, y, z are crystal coordinates; linear uses cosθ x+sinθ z, which is suitable for light propagating along y. ±Circular polarization is defined as (x±iy)/√2, propagating along z. Generally, to superpose polarization, complex amplitudes must be superimposed first, and the intensity cannot be averaged directly. In the axial zero-field model on this page the relevant cross terms disappear and the 45° linear polarization can be used to check the (x+z)/2 intensity.

sections.title: Temperature and external fields change the initial state weight
sections.text: At finite temperature, all initial states are Boltzmann averaged; at T=0, states in a degenerate ground space carry equal weight. A zero-field equilibrium state does not select a magnetization direction, so its circular dichroism should vanish. An applied field along z can produce circular dichroism; reversing the field should exchange the spectra of the two circular polarizations. A single-ion field does not represent the actual antiferromagnetic order of NiO.

lessons.title: From spectrum peak to reviewable absorption report
lessons.summary: distinguishes between relative absorption edges, integrated intensity, broadening and real material spectra, preserving numerical evidence.

sections.title: The zero point of the absorption edge needs to be calibrated independently.
sections.text: Every calculation here takes the energy center of gravity of the final configuration as a reference, and sets the initial ground state energy to zero. The horizontal axis shows the relative transition energy, not the predicted absolute core binding energy; the configuration common displacement brought by F⁰ is eliminated in this coordinate. Chemical shifts cannot be inferred from such recalibrated curves.

sections.title: Broadening changes the peak shape without creating integrated intensity
sections.text: Each line is broadened with a unit-area Lorentzian. Γ is the half width at half maximum, and the full width is 2Γ. A finite energy window truncates tails; outputs give the full-axis intensity, analytical in-window intensity and numerical integral. If the sampling step is too large, the interface asks for a finer grid rather than treating smooth connecting lines as an exact peak profile.

sections.title: Check selection rule with full space
sections.text: For a radial integral of 1, summing over the three orthogonal polarizations x, y, z and a complete final-state space gives an integrated intensity of (2/5) times the number of d holes: 0.8 for d⁸ and 0.4 for d⁹. Divide by 3 for the isotropic average. The noninteracting d⁹ limit with zero valence-shell SOC gives L₃:L₂=2:1; this does not imply the same integrated branching ratio for general multiplets.

exercises.title: Derive the resonance frequency from the field direction
exercises.prompt: S=½, I=0, g=(2,2.1,2.3), B=0.34 T, with no zero-field or hyperfine interaction.

steps.prompt: What is g_eff when the magnetic field points along z?
steps.hint: Keep only nz=1.
steps.explanation: g_eff=|gZ|=2.3。

steps.prompt: What is the approximate frequency?
steps.explanation: ν≈10.9451 GHz. The input already uses H/h, so no additional 2π is needed.

steps.prompt: Keep B fixed and rotate the field to x. Where does the resonance move?
steps.hint: g_eff becomes 2.
steps.explanation: Along x, ν≈9.51745 GHz; the change comes from direction within the same g tensor.

steps.prompt: What happens under parallel microwave drive in a purely isotropic Zeeman model?
steps.hint: The drive contains the same spin component as H.
steps.explanation: The two operators commute, so matrix elements between nondegenerate levels vanish. This does not generalize to every anisotropic model.

exercises.title: Calculate zero-field splitting and electron–nuclear coupling by hand
exercises.prompt: First consider S=1, I=0, B=0, E=0; then compare the isotropic hyperfine model with S=I=½.

steps.prompt: For S=1, what is the D-term energy of mS=0?
steps.explanation: mS=0 has energy −2D/3; mS=±1 has energy D/3.

steps.prompt: For D>0, what is the frequency difference between the two energy groups?
steps.hint: Subtract D/3−(−2D/3).
steps.explanation: The groups are separated by D GHz.

steps.prompt: For S=I=½, B=0, A>0, what are the singlet and triplet energies?
steps.hint: Use total angular momentum F=0 and 1.
steps.explanation: F=0 has energy −3A/4 and F=1 has A/4, separated by A.

steps.prompt: If a multielectron calculation gives a ground-state spin S=1, does it directly determine D?
steps.hint: The low-energy spin dimension does not contain all orbital and SOC information.
choices: No; additional microscopic information or effective parameters are needed
steps.explanation: S specifies the spin space; g, D/E and related parameters require microscopic projection or independent input and cannot automatically be inferred from the current model without SOC.

exercises.title: Assess peak intensities and numerical reliability
exercises.prompt: Fix a pure Zeeman doublet and compare temperature, polarization, linewidth, and mesh.

steps.prompt: Which occupation factor enters net absorption at finite temperature?
steps.hint: Include both absorption and stimulated emission.
steps.explanation: Subtracting the two reverse processes gives net absorption proportional to pi−pf.

steps.prompt: With the energy gap fixed, how does the population difference usually change upon substantial heating?
steps.hint: The two level occupations become closer.
steps.explanation: The equilibrium doublet occupation difference is tanh[Δ/(2kBT)] and decreases with temperature.

steps.prompt: If γ is much smaller than the frequency-grid spacing, can peak heights directly compare intensities?
steps.hint: Sampling may miss the center of a narrow peak.
choices: Look only at the highest plotted point
First refine the grid and check the integrated area
steps.explanation: Comparing analytic window area with discrete integration reveals missed sampling; peak height also depends on linewidth.

steps.prompt: How should the physical spectrum behave after changing eigenvectors within a degenerate level?
steps.hint: Compare the entire subspace rather than arbitrarily selecting one state.
steps.explanation: The sum of projector traces does not depend on basis choice inside a degenerate subspace.

exercises.title: Derivation of subgap conductance from reflection probability
exercises.prompt: Considering the ideal transparent, conventional s-wave NS contact with two physical spins, take the small energy gap approximation, E=0 and eta → 0.

steps.prompt: What is the bulk-quasiparticle transmission T_{qp} into the superconductor inside the gap?
steps.hint: The energy spectrum of the ideal s-wave electrode has a gap at this energy.
steps.explanation: There is no right-propagating bulk-quasiparticle channel, but Andreev processes can still transfer charge.

steps.prompt: is R_{ee}≈0 in the ideal transparency limit, so what is R_{he}?
steps.hint: starts from the conservation of quasiparticle flux.
steps.explanation: T_{qp}=0 and no artificial absorption, so R_{ee}+R_{he}=1, R_{he}=1 is obtained.

steps.prompt: What is 1−R_{ee}+R_{he} for an incident spin channel?
steps.hint: The return hole contribution to the charge current takes the plus sign.
steps.explanation: 1−0+1=2; T_{qp}=0 cannot be used to misjudge the conductance to be 0.

steps.prompt: This page contains two physical spins. What is the final G?
steps.hint: The coefficient of each channel is multiplied by 2e²/h.
steps.explanation: G=2(e²/h)×2=4e²/h. Nambu redundancy no longer adds an additional multiplier.

exercises.title: Put normal devices and NS tools under the same count
exercises.prompt: For a perfectly matched normal chain, take in-band T=1. The existing device-perfect preset counts one spin, while the new tool counts two physical spins. Neglect numerical η.

steps.prompt: What is the G of the old tool device-perfect?
steps.hint: Old default spinDegeneracy=1.
steps.explanation: A single spin and one perfectly transmitting channel give e²/h.

steps.prompt: New tool setting Δ=0, is there reflection from electron to hole?
steps.hint: There is no pairing term to mix the two Nambu components.
steps.explanation: The Hamiltonian separates into electron/hole blocks, so R_{he} is exactly 0.

steps.prompt: What is the G of the new tool Δ=0?
steps.hint: Both physical spins have identical transmission.
steps.explanation: G=2(e²/h)(1−0+0)=2e²/h, divide by 2 to compare to the old single spin preset.

steps.prompt: Subgap enhancement appears only after opening pairing. What is the correct comparison?
steps.hint: controls spin counting and other device parameters.
choices: Use a Δ=0 reference with otherwise identical parameters, and check η
steps.explanation: Keep length, contacts, barrier, μ and numerical η fixed to isolate pairing effects. T_{qp}=0 in the gap, while G can remain nonzero.

exercises.title: Determine whether an NS numerical report is trustworthy
exercises.prompt: A certain subgap is calculated to obtain R_{ee}=.2, R_{he}=.799, T_{qp}=0, and A_η=.001.

steps.prompt: Is the quasiparticle flux closed?
steps.hint: The four terms should add up to 1.
choices: Yes, the sum of the four terms is 1
steps.explanation: contains artificial eta after absorption, .2+.799+0+.001=1.

steps.prompt: Does this prove that eta is small enough?
steps.hint: Conservation equations and physical limit convergence are different requirements.
choices: No; reduce η and compare the results as well
Just check whether the picture is smooth
steps.explanation: Flux conservation can hold despite appreciable artificial absorption; compare η with η/2 and similar values.

steps.prompt: E=Δ returns a null value. What should I do?
steps.hint: This point requires an ideal threshold limit.
choices: Straight line interpolation across empty points to obtain accurate values
Keep null values and compare limits on both sides
steps.explanation: A null value means that this formula does not report a precise threshold and does not mean that the physical conductance is zero.

steps.prompt: How to independently verify the particle-hole relationship?
steps.hint: Compare different incident species with opposite energies.
choices: only checks whether R_{ee}(E) is always 0
steps.explanation: R_{ee}(E)=R_{hh}(−E) under the same agreement, R_{he}(E)=R_{eh}(−E) should be checked at the same time.

exercises.title: Count the initial and final states and identify the core SOC
exercises.prompt: Consider p⁶d⁸→p⁵d⁹, then check p holes in the analytic noninteracting d⁹ limit.

steps.prompt: p⁶d⁸ How many dimensions does the initial state space have?
steps.hint: The p shell is full; choose eight of the ten d spin orbitals.
steps.explanation: C(6,6)C(10,8)=45; the closed p shell adds no extra multiplicity.

steps.prompt: p⁵d⁹ How many dimensions does the final state space have?
steps.hint: selects p-hole and d-hole positions respectively.
steps.explanation: C(6,5)C(10,9)=6×10=60, the six states of the core hole cannot be omitted.

steps.prompt: The j=3/2 energy of p electron ζl·s is +ζ/2; when there is one less electron in the closed shell, what is the hole contribution?
steps.hint: Subtract this electron's contribution from the total full-shell energy.
steps.explanation: The hole energy is the opposite of the electron contribution before it was removed, so the j=3/2 hole is at −ζ/2.

steps.prompt: What are the degeneracies of p holes j=3/2 and j=1/2 respectively?
steps.hint: Use 2j+1.
steps.explanation: The two core branches have 4 and 2 magnetic components; corresponding to the low energy L₃ and the high energy L₂ at the specified analytical limit.

exercises.title: Derivation of polarization contrast from complex amplitudes
exercises.prompt: Same axial model as d⁸, fixing all interactions, temperature and crystal field , changing only light polarization.

steps.prompt: If an energy-level difference lies within the scan window, must an absorption peak appear?
steps.hint: Peak intensities also depend on the initial-state occupations and transition matrix elements.
choices: Not necessarily, the dipole matrix element may be zero
steps.explanation: Energy availability is only one condition; symmetry and wave function can make the amplitude of this polarization zero.

steps.prompt: For ε=(x+z)/√2, which is the general intensity expression?
steps.hint: First linearly superpose the complex amplitudes, and then take the modulus square.
steps.explanation: The first formula retains the interference term; only when the cross term is eliminated by symmetry or averaging, it is equal to the average of the two intensities.

steps.prompt: For zero-field thermal equilibrium and equal weights in degenerate spaces, what check should I₊−I₋ satisfy?
steps.hint: time reversal The circular polarization contributions of the correlated states cancel each other out.
choices: should be zero within numerical error
steps.explanation: Without external fields or spontaneous order, this model remains in time-reversal-invariant equilibrium; axial linear dichroism may still be nonzero.

steps.prompt: Keeping the propagation and polarization conventions unchanged, how should they be compared after inverting the z-direction magnetic field?
steps.hint: time reversal Swap the two circular polarizations.
choices: All spectral peak positions remain unchanged
Add the absolute values of XMCD
steps.explanation: Compare the complete spectrum, not only peak heights. XMCD reversing sign with the field is an important sign check.

exercises.title: Audit integrated intensity, line width and energy zero point
exercises.prompt: has a radial integral of 1, considering the three orthogonal polarizations and the complete final state of the d⁸ atom approximation.

steps.prompt: What is the infinite window integral for the sum of x, y, and z polarizations?
steps.hint: d⁸ has 2 d holes, use (2/5) to multiply the number of holes.
steps.explanation: The three-polarization sum is 0.8; the isotropic average is 0.8/3, and the two normalizations cannot be mixed.

steps.prompt: Γ=0.35 eV is the Lorentz half-width at half-maximum. What is the FWHM?
steps.hint: The full width is the sum of the half-widths on both sides.
steps.explanation: FWHM=2Γ=0.70 eV. Check definitions before comparing experimental broadening.

steps.prompt: The curve area of ​​the finite energy window is smaller than the infinite window intensity. What should be checked first?
steps.hint: Lorentz tail does not strictly zero out at finite energy.
choices: Immediately change the transition matrix elements
steps.explanation: Compare the analytical in-window integral with numerical integration, then enlarge the window; arbitrary normalization must not hide missing intensity.

steps.prompt: only changes F⁰ but this page still resets the edge center of gravity one by one. Can the absolute chemical shift be extracted based on this?
steps.hint: Horizontal axis removed common energy offset between configurations.
choices: Yes, just take the highest peak position
No, independent absorption edge energy calibration is required.
Just increase the number of sampling points
steps.explanation: This model addresses relative multiplet structure and polarization dependence; absolute core-level energies and chemical shifts are outside its scope.

cases.title: Ideal paramagnetic center: rotate the same g tensor
cases.summary: Compare resonance positions and polarization intensities of the same effective S=½ center for different static-field directions.
cases.assumption: g=(2,2.1,2.3) is illustrative and does not specify an actual ion or fitted material. Symmetry constraints alone do not determine numerical g values.

cases.title: Electron and one nucleus: total spin, mixing, and spectral lines
cases.summary: Move from hand-derived zero-field singlet/triplet results to electron–nuclear coupling in a finite magnetic field, observing frequencies and transition intensities.
cases.assumption: Only one S=½ electron spin and one I=½ nuclear spin are included. A is illustrative and does not model a specific molecule's multinuclear spectrum. Microwave driving acts only on the electronic magnetic moment.

cases.title: From a local d⁸ spin to an S=1 spectrum with specified parameters
cases.summary: First establish S=1 in the existing five-orbital model. Then compare effective-spin spectra with D/E disabled and enabled, identifying information missing between the models.
cases.assumption: S=1 comes from the specified d⁸ teaching model. g=2, D=2.87 GHz, and E=0.15 GHz are specified separately. They are not fitted NiO or defect-center parameters and are not automatically derived from this many-electron model without SOC.

cases.assumption: The old device-perfect output is based on one spin; the NS model fixes two physical spins and must be divided by 2 before comparison. The numerical difference eta absorption needs to be retained.

cases.title: Transparent interface and potential barrier: same energy gap, different conductance
cases.summary: Compare the no-barrier and single-point barrier curves side by side and observe normal reflection, hole reflection, and charge response.
cases.assumption: parameters are teaching values, fixed potential, zero temperature and no magnetic field/SOC; do not represent a quantitative fit of specific aluminum, niobium or semiconductor contacts.

cases.title: Thresholds and artificial absorption: writing diagnoses into reports
cases.summary: compares the precise energy gap threshold, energy on both sides and eta changes to distinguish the real propagation channel and numerical broadening.
cases.assumption: This experiment does not introduce superconducting lead broadening; the threshold null point is not the actual conductance of 0, nor can a single subgap peak be used to declare the Majorana state.

cases.summary: connects the existing d⁸ Kanamori background to the complete Slater/SOC atomic approximation, identifying energy levels, core holes and transition strengths.
cases.kind: Real material background + original ion model
cases.assumption: The parameters are not fitted to NiO. Ligand-to-metal charge transfer, antiferromagnetic order, and the experimental absolute absorption edge are excluded. The earlier U/J parameters cannot be mapped term by term onto the Slater integrals used here.

cases.kind: Free ion limit that can be calculated by hand
cases.assumption: This is an analytic benchmark for d⁹, not a prediction of the CuO spectrum. Branching intensities for general multiplets require the full transition calculation.
